Introduction to Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)

RAG is a technique that combines information retrieval with large language model generation.
Instead of relying solely on the model's trained knowledge, RAG fetches relevant documents
from a knowledge base and uses them as context when generating answers.

How RAG Works:
1. The user submits a question.
2. The question is converted into an embedding (a vector representation).
3. The embedding is used to search a vector database for similar document chunks.
4. The top-K most relevant chunks are retrieved.
5. These chunks are passed as context to the LLM along with the question.
6. The LLM generates an answer grounded in the retrieved context.

Benefits of RAG:
- Reduces hallucinations by grounding answers in real documents.
- Allows the model to access up-to-date or domain-specific information.
- Provides source citations so users can verify answers.
- Works with smaller, cheaper models since knowledge is external.

Vector Databases:
A vector database stores embeddings (numerical representations of text) and allows
fast similarity search. ChromaDB is a popular local vector database used in RAG systems.
It supports cosine similarity search and can persist data to disk.

Embedding Models:
Text embeddings convert sentences and paragraphs into high-dimensional vectors.
Similar pieces of text will have similar vectors. The nomic-embed-text model produces
768-dimensional vectors and runs locally via Ollama.

Local LLMs with Ollama:
Ollama makes it easy to run large language models locally on consumer hardware.
Models like llama3.2:3b (3 billion parameters) can run on a CPU-only machine with 8GB RAM.
This enables fully private, offline AI applications.
